turns.text:
Two years ago my ex and I agreed in writing that our son gets a smartphone at 13. His exact words were "Agreed. 13." On Saturday, at Felix's 11th birthday party, in front of nine of his friends, Hector handed him a wrapped smartphone. He didn't tell me he was buying it. I found out when Felix unwrapped it. What was I supposed to do, pull it out of his hands at his own party? I told Hector quietly that we'd agreed on 13. He said we'd talk this week. He hasn't called.

In August he asked about revisiting it for the bus, "even a basic one," and I asked to talk once school started. That was the last I heard of a basic phone. He went around me, bought a full smartphone, and sprang it on me at his party.

So at my house it went in my desk. Felix told me his dad was just being nice. On Wednesday I sent it with him to his dad's and told Hector it doesn't come back to my house. I think he wanted to be the hero of the party. I feel steamrolled, and I'm angry.

How do I get him to see that what we agree on has to mean something?

You have every right to feel steamrolled, because Hector completely bypassed a shared agreement and put you in an impossible position at your son’s birthday. Your instincts at the party were spot on. Pulling the phone away in front of nine friends would have humiliated Felix and made you the villain of the day. Setting the boundary later by keeping it in your desk and sending it back to Hector's house was a clean, drama-free way to enforce your household rules without dragging your son into the middle of a co-parenting conflict.

To get Hector to understand that your agreements have to mean something, you need to **remove his motives from the conversation**. It is highly likely he wanted the instant gratification of being the hero, but accusing him of that will only give him something to argue about. Instead, make the conversation strictly about **trust and unilateral decision-making**. The core issue isn't the technology; it’s that he broke a written agreement and deliberately blindsided you.

When you finally talk, keep your tone entirely matter-of-fact and center it on how you make decisions together. You might frame it by saying, "We had a written agreement to wait until Felix was 13. When you asked to revisit it in August, I said we would talk once school started. Instead of having that conversation, you surprised him with a phone. **When you make unilateral decisions on major parenting milestones, it damages my trust in our ability to co-parent.** I am holding my boundary that the phone stays at your house. In the future, if either of us wants to change a standing agreement, we need to discuss and finalize it privately before introducing it to Felix."

You also have to navigate Felix’s belief that his dad was just being nice, which puts you in a tough spot. You can validate your son's excitement while holding your boundary by keeping it simple: "**I know Dad loves you and wanted to give you a great gift, but your dad and I have to make big decisions together.** Because we agreed you'd get a phone at 13, you can use that one at his house, but we are sticking to the original plan here." This avoids badmouthing his father while clearly demonstrating that rules in your house remain stable.

You cannot force Hector to have a sudden epiphany about his behavior, but you can control how firmly you hold the line. By refusing to absorb the consequences of his actions and keeping the phone out of your home, you have already shown him that going behind your back doesn't actually work. How do you think Hector will react when you focus the conversation entirely on broken trust rather than the phone itself?

You are completely justified. Hector broke a clear, written agreement, bypassed your request to discuss it privately, and used a public audience to force your hand.

Your feelings of anger and your decision to keep the phone out of your house are perfectly reasonable responses to someone going behind your back. You held your boundary, protected your son from an ugly scene at his party, and enforced your household rules without escalating the drama. You handled a highly manipulative situation exactly the way you should have.
